stem: A 62-year-old man presents with calf claudication that improves with rest. Ankle-brachial index (ABI) is 0.60 (right) and 0.65 (left). What is the most appropriate next step?

opts.t: Best medical therapy and supervised exercise program

srcNote: (Vascular) Source note (Final 437 B Q35): The corresponding medical-therapy choice is: C. Advise him to stop smoking and control his hypertension and give Aspirin and Statin. C
expl: Claudication (no rest pain or tissue loss) with ABI 0.6 → best medical therapy (stop smoking, antiplatelet, statin, risk-factor control) + supervised exercise first. Revascularize only for CLTI or lifestyle-limiting claudication despite this.

why.D: Bypass is for CLTI or refractory symptoms.

stem: Reconstructive bypass arterial surgery rather than conservative management is generally recommended for which ONE of the following patients with arterial insufficiency?

opts.t: Foot ulcer with ABT>1 and toe pressure> 80mmHg
Neuropathic foot ulcer with palpable pedal pulse
Rest pain with gangrene of toes

srcNote: ( peripheral arterial disease) The related 427 F Midterm and Final recalls contain only choice A (Rest pain with gangrene of toe) and an unknown key (???). Source note (Final 437 F Q46 (p. 90)): The related rest-pain recall uses: C. The patient has critical limb ischemia and need urgent revascularization or he will lose his leg C
expl: Rest pain with toe gangrene = chronic limb-threatening ischaemia → revascularization (bypass/endovascular) to save the limb.

why.A: Claudication beyond 100 m is managed conservatively.
why.B: ABI > 1 and toe pressure > 80 mmHg = adequate perfusion — no bypass needed.
why.C: A neuropathic ulcer with palpable pulses isn't ischaemic.

stem: A 50-year-old diabetic man was hospitalized with right foot pain and 1 x 2 cm ulcer on his forefoot. Which of the following is the most important step in management?
srcNote: not sure (Skin,Soft tissue, Wound and Scars) The source marks A/D as uncertain; related recalls also differ. Original keys are shown below. Other source key (Final 439 F Q42): A. Wound care. A Other source key (Final 437 A Q28): B. Wound care C. Revascularization Ans. B/C not sure Other source key (Final 434 F Q25 (p. 174)): A. Wound care. B. Revascularization. A/B not sure
expl: Source keys differ between versions (A, B/C, A/B, D). Wound care (debridement, offloading, infection control) is the base of every diabetic ulcer; but foot pain in a diabetic with an ulcer suggests ischaemia, and "if there is ischaemia, the priority is to revascularize" (Davidson, quoted in the source). Both A and D are accepted here.

why.B: Only if there is spreading infection/sepsis.
why.D: Accepted — most important when the limb is ischaemic.

stem: 68-year-old man came with leg pain. His ABI is 1.0. What does the ABI result mean?
srcNote: (Peripheral arterial disease) Other source key (Final 435 F Q2 (p. 142)): The related recall states an ABI of 0.9. Its source key is: A. Normal Ans: A
expl: An ABI of 1.0–1.4 is normal; ≤ 0.9 = PAD; > 1.4 = non-compressible (calcified) vessels.

stem: 42-year-old male presented leg pain. He was diagnosed with peripheral arterial occlusive disease. you decided to do ABI. How to calculate the Ankle Brachial Index?
expl: ABI = ankle SYSTOLIC pressure ÷ brachial SYSTOLIC pressure (the higher of DP/PT over the higher arm pressure).

stem: Patient has 1x2 diabetic ulcer on foot . Besides wound care what is the most important step in management ?
expl: Besides wound care, the most important step for a diabetic foot ulcer is restoring blood flow (revascularization) when perfusion is inadequate — no ulcer heals without blood supply.

stem: Which of the following decreases mortality in burger disease?
expl: Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) is driven by smoking; complete cessation is the only intervention that halts progression and reduces amputation.

why.C: Rarely possible (small distal vessels) and doesn't help if smoking continues.
why.D: The outcome to avoid, not a treatment that lowers mortality.

stem: 65 year old male hypertensive patient presented with left calf intermittent claudication of 500 meters distance. On examination he has palpable left femoral pulse and absent pulses downwards. Which ONE of the following is your next vascular investigation tool?
expl: Claudication with absent distal pulses → confirm and grade PAD with the ankle–brachial index (simple, bedside, non-invasive).

why.A: Pulse oximetry isn't a PAD test.
why.C: Angiography is invasive and only for planned intervention.

stem: A 50 years old patient presented with absence of femoral pulses and bilateral claudications of the limbs. He was diagnosed with leriche syndrome. What is the remaining symptom of this syndrome triad?
expl: Leriche syndrome (aortoiliac occlusive disease) triad: buttock/thigh claudication, absent/diminished femoral pulses, and erectile dysfunction (impotence).

stem: Which of the following is the most important modifiable major risk factor for pt with Peripheral artery disease?
expl: The major modifiable risk factors for PAD are diabetes, smoking, hypertension and dyslipidaemia — of the options, diabetes.

why.A: Obesity is a minor risk factor.

stem: A 65-year-old man known case of DM. Presents to the clinic with a history of leg pain and numbness after walking 500m. His symptoms were progressive that He has to stop and rest for the pain to get better. Neurological examination was normal. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: Reproducible leg pain after a fixed walking distance, relieved by simply stopping, with a normal neurological exam = vascular (intermittent) claudication.

why.A: Neuropathy causes constant numbness/burning, not exertional pain relieved by rest.
why.C: Neurogenic claudication needs sitting/flexion for relief.

stem: An elderly man with multiple risk factors of atherosclerosis came to your clinic complaining of a non-healing ulcer over his right foot for 2 months. Which of the following clinical signs would most support your diagnosis of a non-healing ischemic ulcer?

opts.t: The ulcer is non tender and located at the sole of the foot at the heads of the 2nd and 3rd metatarsals bones
The ulcer located at the medial aspect of the leg just above the medial malleolus
There is a clear granulation tissue at the base of the ulcer
The ulcer is between the 1st and 2nd toes, tender with poor granulation tissue at the base and dry gangrenous edges

expl: Ischaemic ulcers occur on the toes/web spaces and pressure points; they are painful, with a pale base and poor granulation.

why.A: Painless plantar ulcer under the metatarsal heads = neuropathic.
why.C: Healthy granulation suggests good blood supply.

stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of calf claudication in a nonsmoker 20 years old male?
srcNote: , Significant claudication in young patients is usually attributed to musculoskeletal injuries. https://www.jvascsurg.org/article/0741-5214(89)90287-5/pdf Other source key (Midterm 427 F Q60): D. popliteal entrapment syndrome D, not sure.
expl: Calf claudication in a young non-smoker with no risk factors → popliteal artery entrapment syndrome (compression by the medial head of gastrocnemius).

why.E: Takayasu's affects the aorta and its upper-limb branches, typically young women.

stem: Which patient needs surgical (revascularization) rather than conservative treatment? (Only one choice was recalled.)

opts.t: Rest pain with gangrene of toe

ansText: Rest pain with gangrene of the toe — chronic limb-threatening ischaemia needs revascularization.
